n: A few dead flies can make expensive perfume stink. In the same way, a little foolishness can ruin the reputation of someone known for wisdom.
A wise heart leans toward what is right, while a fool’s heart leans the wrong way. The right hand symbolized strength and favor in the ancient world.
Even walking down the road, a fool shows his lack of sense and makes his foolishness obvious to everyone.

f.g: Literally “his heart is lacking” — he lacks sense.

n: If a ruler gets angry with you, don’t quit your post. Calm and gentleness can settle even great offenses.
The Preacher notes a kind of mistake rulers make.
Fools get promoted to high positions while capable, wealthy people are given lowly places.

f.g: Here the noble or capable, in contrast to fools.

n: He has seen servants riding horses like nobles, and princes walking on foot like servants — a world turned upside down.
Every task carries risk: one who digs a pit may fall in, and one who breaks through a stone wall may be bitten by a snake hiding there. Plotting harm often backfires.

f.g: A stone wall, where snakes often hid.

n: Quarrying stones or splitting wood can injure the worker. Life calls for caution and skill.
A dull axe takes more effort; sharpening it first is smarter. Wisdom helps people succeed with less wasted strength.
If a snake bites before it is charmed, the snake charmer gains nothing. Skill is useless if not used at the right time.

f.g: Literally “master of the tongue” — the charmer.

n: A wise person’s words are kind and win favor, but a fool’s own talk destroys him.
A fool’s speech starts in foolishness and ends in destructive madness.
Fools talk on and on, though no one knows the future or what happens after them.
A fool’s work wears him out because he can’t even find his way to town. He lacks basic common sense.
Pity the nation whose king is immature and whose leaders feast in the morning instead of working.

f.g: Party when they should be judging and working.

n: Happy is the nation whose king is noble and whose leaders eat at the proper time, for strength rather than drunkenness.
Through laziness the roof sags, and idle hands let the house leak. Neglect slowly ruins homes — and nations.
Feasts bring laughter and wine brings cheer, but money pays for everything. The verse may be a sly comment on careless leaders.

f.g: Money meets every demand — often read ironically.

n: Don’t curse the king even in your thoughts or the rich even in private, because word gets around in unexpected ways. The saying “a little bird told me” comes from this idea.

f.w: a bird of the air shall carry the voice
f.g: Secrets have a way of spreading.
